title: Pip and the Wishing Stones
markdown:
Pip the rabbit lived in a snug burrow at the edge of Sunny Meadow. His fur was the colour of warm toast. His whiskers did a little jig when he was happy, or when he was thinking very hard. He loved his burrow, his neat rows of carrots, the familiar chirping of meadow birds. He liked his days predictable: dewy grass, the satisfying crunch of a perfectly grown carrot.

One morning something was amiss. The wishing stones — a cluster of smooth grey rocks in the village square where everyone whispered secret hopes — were cold. Usually they hummed with a soft warmth, like a teacup on a chilly day. Today they felt like pebbles from a cold stream, lifeless. A ripple shivered through Pip's paws. Facing anything new felt prickly. He wanted everything to stay the same. He did not like talking to strangers about it.

"Oh dear," he sighed, tucking his ears back.

He knew he had to do something. The Whispering Woods waited: deep shadows, rustling leaves that always sounded like secrets. His nose twitched. The midsummer parade was two days away. The stones had to be warm for the parade's special magic. If they weren't, the parade would be a bit dim. Pip could not bear a dim parade.

He took a breath that smelled of damp earth and sweet clover and hopped toward the dark edge of the woods. Trees stood tall, branches like reaching fingers. Sunlight moved on moss. His heart thumped a little faster. He kept his eyes on the path, paws careful over leaves that crunched like old paper. Cooler air, mossy ancient bark. He almost turned around. The rustling sounded like a hundred voices urging him back to carrots.

Deep in, where the air grew still, he heard a tiny sputtering, a weak little fire trying to stay alight. He tiptoed, fluffy tail low, and peeked through thick green ferns.

Huddled beside the largest coldest wishing stone was the tiniest dragon he had ever seen, no bigger than Pip's thumb, scales like a rainbow after rain. The dragon puffed little clouds of warm air, scales glowing ember-soft. Pip gasped, a gentle squeak. He recognised him: Marlo, who lived in a secret nook in a hollow log, known for being very, very shy, even more so than Pip.

Marlo flinched. Wings fluttered. He had not expected anyone.

Pip wanted to hop away. He saw Marlo's tiny sad eyes. He remembered the cold grey stones. Marlo shivered ever so slightly, trying his very best.

"Hello," Pip whispered.

Marlo jumped. His puff fizzled. "Oh. H-hello." Tiny bells, shaky. Wide curious eyes.

"Why are you puffing?"

Marlo's shoulders slumped. He kicked a pebble. "I like the wishing stones. They're usually so warm and happy. They were getting cold, so I've been using my fire to keep them from freezing. It's not much, but it's all I have." He shivered again. His glow was dimmer than usual, a candle in a draft. The warmth he gave off felt very weak.

Pip's eyes widened. He had found why the stones were cold. Helping meant asking Marlo to share precious warmth. "Marlo. The wishing stones need to be warm for the parade. Your fire is good, but the moon's light isn't reaching them. A grumpy cloud has been sitting on the sky for days, blocking the moonbeams."

"A grumpy cloud? Oh dear. That sounds very bothersome."

"Your fire is the only thing that can relight them. But if you keep using it, you'll get very cold. You might even get chilly."

Pip wrung his paws. His own fur felt warm and safe. Marlo looked at the dull stones, then at Pip's kind face. He understood.

"I will," Marlo said, a little spark of determination. "I'll share my warmth. I don't want the parade to be dim."

He took a breath, a rumble in his chest, and puffed. Stronger. Focused. Soft heat. The stones began to glow, faint warm light, embers catching. A scent of singed grass. Wings trembled. Marlo's scales dimmed. A shiver rattled him. Pip hopped closer and nudged him. The scales felt cool — a stark contrast to the warmth going into the stones.

That was the cost: Marlo's own fire, given away by the puff.

"Thank you, Marlo." Pip meant it. "Now we must hurry. The parade starts soon."

He scooped Marlo into his pocket, comfortable as a burrow. Marlo snuggled, little dragon snores a faint warmth against Pip's side.

They hurried back through the Whispering Woods. The path that had sounded like a hundred voices now sounded only like leaves. Sun dipping, orange and pink on the clouds. Marlo's pocket-snores kept time with Pip's hops. The village was buzzing with excited chatter, but everyone looked a little disappointed at the dull wishing stones — until Pip and Marlo emerged from the trees. The stones were no longer cold. They glowed with a soft steady warmth, Marlo's brave little fire still in them.

Pip, no longer hiding, hopped to the centre of the square. He stood tall, fluffy tail high. "Everyone!" he announced, his voice clear and strong, surprising even himself. "This is Marlo! He kept the wishing stones warm for us! He's a wonderful pocket dragon!"

Marlo peeked out of the pocket, scales still a little dim, a happy twinkle in his bright eyes. The villagers cheered. Mrs. Higgins's buns, cooling on a sill, seemed to cheer too, in a yeasty way. A new warmth spread through Marlo that had nothing to do with his own fire: being appreciated, making friends. Pip looked up and saw Mrs. Higgins waving a floury paw. Instead of hiding, Pip wiggled his nose and waved back.

The stones hummed their teacup hum again. The grumpy cloud, if it was still up there, had lost the argument. Pip's whiskers did a happy jig, and Marlo, in the pocket, was a small extra heartbeat, cooling, brave, and — for the first time — not only a secret in a log.
